Key Points
sections.content:
- **`groupingBy`/`partitioningBy`** with downstream collectors is the 80% use case.
- **`mapping`**, **`filtering`** (Java 9+), **`reducing`**, **`collectingAndThen`** compose with `groupingBy`.
- **`summarizingInt/Long/Double`** gives count, sum, min, max, avg in one pass.
- **`toMap`** requires a **merge function** for duplicate keys — otherwise throws `IllegalStateException`.
- **`teeing`** (Java 12+) runs two collectors and merges their results.
- **Custom collector**: `Collector.of(supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher)`.
- **`CONCURRENT + UNORDERED + IDENTITY_FINISH`** enables maximum parallel throughput on thread-safe accumulators.
- **Prefer composition** over custom collectors — clearer code; write custom only when needed.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Beyond `toList`, `toSet`, and `toMap`, the power of `Collectors` comes from **composition**. The 80% use case is **`groupingBy`** with a **downstream collector**.

For example, instead of grouping into a `Map<Status, List<Order>>` and then streaming each list to sum the amounts, I do it in one pass: `groupingBy(Order::getStatus, reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, Order::getAmount, BigDecimal::add))`.

The most-useful advanced collectors I reach for are **`summarizingInt/Long/Double`** — gives count, sum, min, max, and average in a single pass — **`mapping`** to transform elements into the downstream collector, **`filtering`** (Java 9+) to filter within groups while keeping empty groups, **`collectingAndThen`** to post-process (typically `unmodifiableList`), and **`teeing`** (Java 12+) to run two collectors in parallel and merge their results.

For **custom collectors**, `Collector.of(supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher)` is the shortcut over implementing the full interface. The four parts: **supplier** creates the accumulator, **accumulator** folds one element in, **combiner** merges two accumulators for parallel execution, and **finisher** converts the accumulator to the final result. Plus **characteristics** — `CONCURRENT`, `UNORDERED`, `IDENTITY_FINISH` — which are optimization hints for parallel streams.

A practical example of writing a custom collector: **variance calculation** — you need to track count, sum, and sum-of-squares together. That's three metrics in one pass, which no built-in collector gives you directly.

**When to write custom vs compose**: I compose by default. Writing custom only makes sense for truly novel aggregations or when targeting a third-party container like a Guava `ImmutableList`. For most 'how do I aggregate X from a stream' problems, the answer is a nested `groupingBy` with the right downstream collector.

questions.question: When should you use parallel streams in Java? What are the trade-offs and pitfalls?
questions.title: When to Use Parallel Streams — Trade-offs, Pitfalls, and Better Alternatives
questions.direct_answer: Use **parallel streams** only when **all** of these are true: (1) the work is **CPU-bound** (not I/O), (2) the dataset is **large enough** (rule of thumb: 10K+ elements with non-trivial per-element work), (3) the source **splits efficiently** (`ArrayList`, arrays, `IntStream.range` — not `LinkedList` or `Files.lines`), (4) operations are **stateless and side-effect-free**, and (5) you can tolerate the result being on **`ForkJoinPool.commonPool`**, which is shared JVM-wide. The biggest pitfall: people slap `.parallel()` on everything assuming "more threads = faster." Often it's slower because of split overhead, lousy splitter, or contention. Worst-case: I/O inside a parallel stream blocks `commonPool` workers — every other parallel stream and `CompletableFuture.runAsync()` in the JVM stalls. **Better alternatives**: for I/O-bound concurrency use `CompletableFuture` with a dedicated `Executor`; on Java 21+, virtual threads via `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` scale to millions of blocking tasks. Parallel streams shine for batch CPU work (image processing, encryption, large numeric reductions); benchmark with **JMH**, never assume.

sections.title: What Parallel Streams Actually Do
sections.content:
Calling `.parallel()` (or starting with `.parallelStream()`) tells the Stream API to split the source into chunks, process them concurrently on multiple threads, and merge results.

**Default execution pool**: `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, which has `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1` worker threads (one less than the core count). The same pool is shared by **every parallel stream and every `CompletableFuture.xxxAsync()` (without an explicit executor)** in the JVM.

**The work-splitting mechanism** is the **Spliterator**:
- Source's spliterator splits the data into chunks (`trySplit`).
- Each chunk is processed on a worker thread.
- Stateless operations (`filter`, `map`) parallelize cleanly.
- Stateful operations (`sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) introduce barriers and merging.
- Terminal operation merges per-thread results (`reduce`, `collect`, etc.).

**Sources that split well**: `ArrayList`, arrays, `IntStream.range(...)`, `LongStream.rangeClosed(...)`. They have known size and random access, so splitting is O(1).

**Sources that split poorly**: `LinkedList`, `Stream.iterate`, `Files.lines`, `BufferedReader.lines`. They're sequential by nature; the splitter has to read elements to chunk them, which often defeats the parallelism.

sections.title: When Parallel Streams Help — The Sweet Spot
sections.content:
**Pattern**: large dataset, CPU-bound per-element work, splittable source, stateless ops.

```java
// Image processing batch — CPU-heavy per element
List<Image> processed = imageList.parallelStream()
    .map(img -> applyFilters(img))   // CPU-heavy: convolution, encoding
    .map(img -> compress(img))
    .toList();
```

```java
// Large numeric reduction
long primeCount = IntStream.rangeClosed(2, 10_000_000)
    .parallel()
    .filter(this::isPrime)
    .count();
```

```java
// Mathematical aggregation across millions
double[] data = new double[10_000_000];
// ... populate ...
double sum = Arrays.stream(data).parallel().sum();
```

```java
// Hashing many records
List<String> hashes = passwords.parallelStream()
    .map(this::bcryptHash)   // CPU-bound
    .toList();
```

**Sweet-spot characteristics**:
- 10K+ elements (or fewer with very heavy per-element work).
- Per-element cost dominates split/merge overhead.
- Source splits in O(1): `ArrayList`, array, `IntStream.range`.
- Stateless ops only — no `sorted` or `limit` mid-pipeline.
- No I/O, no shared mutable state, no thread-affine resources.
- You can tolerate the work running on `commonPool`.

sections.title: When Parallel Streams Hurt — The Anti-Patterns
The commonPool Trap
Spliterator and Source Splittability
sections.content:
The source's `Spliterator` decides how the work splits. The Stream API calls `trySplit()` repeatedly to subdivide work; the better the splitter, the better the parallelism.

**Splittability ratings**:

| Source | Split quality | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `ArrayList`, `Vector` | Excellent | O(1) split, known size, random access |
| Array (`Arrays.stream`) | Excellent | Same as above |
| `IntStream.range`, `LongStream.range` | Excellent | O(1) split, known size |
| `HashSet`, `HashMap.keySet/values/entrySet` | Good | Internal arrays of buckets, splits well |
| `TreeMap`, `TreeSet` | Good | Tree-based, decent split |
| `LinkedList`, `LinkedHashSet` | Poor | No random access, O(n) split |
| `Stream.iterate`, `Stream.generate` | Poor | Sequential by definition |
| `Files.lines`, `BufferedReader.lines` | Poor | Sequential I/O source |

**Custom spliterators**: you can implement `Spliterator<T>` to make custom sources splittable, but it's tricky. Most code just uses `parallelStream()` on `ArrayList`/array sources where it works well by default.

**Test it**: use `stream.spliterator().characteristics()` to see flags like `SIZED`, `ORDERED`, `DISTINCT`. The presence of `SIZED` enables faster splits.

sections.title: Java 21 — Virtual Threads Change the Calculus
Decision Guide — Should I Use Parallel Streams?
sections.content:
**Use parallel streams when ALL of these are true**:
- Work is **CPU-bound** (no I/O, no DB, no network).
- Dataset is **large** (rule of thumb: 10K+ elements).
- Per-element cost is **non-trivial** (more than a few microseconds).
- Source **splits well**: `ArrayList`, array, `IntStream.range`, `HashMap.entrySet`.
- Operations are **stateless and associative**.
- No shared mutable state in lambdas.
- You're **OK sharing `commonPool`** with the rest of the JVM.
- You can **measure** the speedup (with JMH).

**Don't use parallel streams when**:
- Work involves I/O (HTTP, DB, file). Use `CompletableFuture` + sized executor, or virtual threads on Java 21+.
- Dataset is small (< few thousand elements with cheap ops).
- Source splits poorly (`LinkedList`, `Files.lines`, `Stream.iterate`).
- Pipeline has heavy stateful ops (`sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) at scale.
- Your lambdas mutate shared state.
- Per-element cost is microseconds and hardware is busy.
- You haven't benchmarked.

**Better alternatives**:
- **I/O-bound concurrency**: `CompletableFuture` with `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(N)`, or virtual threads (Java 21+).
- **Mixed CPU+I/O pipeline**: split into stages — do CPU sequentially or with small parallel stream, do I/O with virtual threads.
- **Specialized parallel computation**: `ForkJoinTask` directly, or libraries like `parallel-streams-utils`.
- **Async batch jobs**: actor frameworks (Akka), reactive (Project Reactor, RxJava) for backpressure-aware streams.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Parallel streams** split the source via `Spliterator`, process chunks on `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`.
- **`commonPool` size**: cores - 1 (typically 7 on an 8-core box).
- **Sweet spot**: CPU-bound work, large dataset (10K+), splittable source, stateless ops.
- **Worst pitfall**: I/O inside parallel stream blocks the commonPool, stalling the whole JVM.
- **Splittability**: `ArrayList`, arrays, `IntStream.range` — great. `LinkedList`, `Files.lines` — terrible.
- **Stateful ops** (`sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) create barriers and serialize work.
- **Shared mutable state in lambdas** → race conditions; use collectors instead.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Parallel streams are tempting — just call `.parallel()` and your code goes faster, right? Often the opposite. They're great for a narrow window: CPU-bound batch work over large, splittable datasets. Outside that window they're slower or actively harmful.

**What parallel streams actually do**
- Source's `Spliterator` splits the data into chunks
- Chunks run on `ForkJoinPool.commonPool` (typically cores - 1 = ~7 worker threads on an 8-core box)
- Stateless ops (filter, map) parallelize cleanly
- Stateful ops (sorted, distinct, limit) introduce barriers
- Terminal op (`collect`, `reduce`) merges per-thread results
- All `.parallelStream()` calls and `CompletableFuture.xxxAsync()` calls in the JVM share the same commonPool

**Sweet spot — use parallel streams when**
- Work is **CPU-bound** — no I/O, no DB, no network
- Dataset is **large** — rule of thumb: 10K+ elements
- Per-element cost is **non-trivial** — microseconds at minimum
- Source **splits well** — `ArrayList`, array, `IntStream.range`, `HashMap.entrySet`
- Operations are **stateless and side-effect-free**
- Examples: image processing batch, hashing many records, large numeric reductions, prime counting

**Anti-patterns — don't use parallel streams when**

**1. I/O-bound work — worst pitfall**
- HTTP calls or DB queries inside `.parallelStream().map(...)` block commonPool workers
- 8-core box → ~7 worker threads — a single 10s HTTP call kills 1/7 of capacity
- Every other parallel stream in the JVM stalls
- Fix: `CompletableFuture` with sized executor, or virtual threads on Java 21

**2. Shared mutable state**
- `result.add(x)` from parallel lambdas — race condition
- Use collectors (`.toList()`, `.collect(...)`) instead — thread-safe by design

**3. Small datasets**
- Splitting and merging overhead exceeds the work
- Sequential wins

**4. Poor splitters**
- `LinkedList` — no random access, O(n) split
- `Files.lines`, `Stream.iterate` — sequential by nature
- Parallel often slower than sequential here

**5. Stateful ops**
- `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit` create barriers
- Most work serializes around them

**The commonPool trap**
- One module's blocking misuse can stall the entire JVM
- Tuning `-Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N` masks the problem
- Wrapping in a custom `ForkJoinPool` works but is verbose; usually a code smell

**Java 21 changes the game**
- Virtual threads make `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` the right tool for I/O-bound concurrency
- Scale to millions of blocking tasks; ~few hundred bytes vs 1MB per platform thread
- No commonPool saturation, no pool sizing
- Parallel streams remain useful for CPU-bound batch work

**Better alternatives**
- I/O-bound: `CompletableFuture` + `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50)`, or virtual threads (Java 21+)
- Massive concurrency: virtual threads — millions of blocking tasks
- Mixed CPU+I/O: split into stages — CPU sequential or small parallel, I/O via virtual threads
- Backpressure-aware: Project Reactor or RxJava

**Recommendation:** My default is **sequential streams**. I switch to parallel only when I have a concrete signal: a large dataset (10K+ elements), heavy per-element CPU work (image processing, encryption, prime counting), and a splittable source (`ArrayList`, array, `IntStream.range`). I always **benchmark with JMH** before committing — perceived speedup is often noise. For I/O-bound work, I never use parallel streams; on Java 17 it's `CompletableFuture` with a sized `Executor`, on Java 21+ it's `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`. If I genuinely need parallel streams isolated from commonPool, I wrap them in a custom `ForkJoinPool` — but that's usually a sign I should restructure the code. The mental model: parallel streams are a sharp tool for CPU batch jobs, not a general-purpose "make code faster" button.

sections.title: Parallel Streams Are Rarely the Right Tool
sections.content:
Parallel streams are one of Java's most **misunderstood** features. The API makes it trivially easy — change `stream()` to `parallelStream()` — which has convinced many developers that parallel is a free speedup. It isn't. For most real workloads, parallel streams either provide no benefit or actively hurt performance.

The reasons:

1. **All parallel streams share the common ForkJoinPool** — `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` with `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1` threads by default. Every `parallelStream()` anywhere in your JVM competes for those threads. One slow parallel stream blocks all others.

2. **Parallelization has fixed overhead** — splitting the source, coordinating threads, merging results. For small collections or short per-element work, this overhead dominates.

3. **The common pool is not for blocking work** — it's sized for CPU-bound tasks. Putting a JDBC call or HTTP call inside a parallel stream's `map` occupies a common-pool thread for the blocking duration, starving other parallel streams.

4. **Ordering and state are subtle** — `forEach` on a parallel stream processes elements in an unspecified order; if you mutate shared state, you'll see races. `findFirst` has an order-coordination cost that `findAny` doesn't.

The honest rule: **don't parallelize until you've measured and proved sequential is the bottleneck**. Even then, consider a dedicated `ForkJoinPool` or `ExecutorService` instead of the common pool.

sections.title: The NQ Model — When Parallelization Pays Off
sections.content:
Doug Lea (author of `ForkJoinPool`) describes a simple model for predicting parallel speedup: the **NQ product**, where **N** is the number of elements and **Q** is the work per element (roughly, time in nanoseconds).

**Rule of thumb**: parallelization pays when `N × Q > ~10,000` — in other words, enough total work to amortize coordination overhead.

- N=1,000,000 and Q=10ns (simple map) → N×Q = 10,000,000 → parallel likely faster
- N=1,000 and Q=100ns → N×Q = 100,000 → marginal; measure
- N=100 and Q=10μs → N×Q = 1,000,000 → parallel likely faster
- N=100,000 and Q=5ns (primitive add) → N×Q = 500,000 → measure; probably not worth it

**Per-element work that is typically parallelizable**:
- Heavy computation: hashing, compression, image processing, numerical simulation
- Complex object transformations that involve real work

**Per-element work that typically isn't worth parallelizing**:
- Simple arithmetic on primitives — sequential tight loops beat parallel streams handily
- Getter/setter chains on POJOs
- Anything that spends most time in the JIT-ed method call overhead itself

**Source split efficiency** also matters hugely. The `Spliterator` characteristics determine how well a source parallelizes:

| Source | Splitting | Parallel Performance |
|---|---|---|
| `ArrayList`, `int[]`, `long[]` | Index-based, O(1) | Excellent |
| `HashMap.entrySet()` | Reasonable | Good |
| `LinkedList` | Sequential scan | Poor — forces sequential-like behavior |
| `Stream.iterate()` | Sequential | Unparallelizable |
| `Files.lines()` | Sequential read | Poor |
| `IntStream.range()` | Index-based | Excellent |

questions.title: `reduce` vs `collect` — Immutable Folding vs Mutable Reduction
questions.direct_answer: Both `reduce` and `collect` are **terminal operations that combine stream elements into a single result**, but they work very differently. **`reduce(identity, accumulator)`** repeatedly applies a binary operator to fold elements into one value — it expects an **immutable accumulator** (each step returns a new value). It's perfect for **scalar reductions**: sum, max, multiply, string concatenation (small inputs), or computing a single derived value. **`collect(supplier, accumulator, combiner)`** uses a **mutable container** that accumulates elements in place — it's perfect for **building collections** (`List`, `Set`, `Map`) or other mutable structures. **The performance rule**: don't use `reduce` to build collections. `reduce(emptyList, (l, x) -> { l2 = new ArrayList(l); l2.add(x); return l2; }, ...)` is O(n²) because every step copies the list. `collect(toList())` is O(n) because it appends to a single list. **The semantic rule**: use `reduce` when the result type is the same as the element type (or a simple derived value); use `collect` when you're building a structure. **When in doubt**: for collections, use `Collectors.toList()`/`toSet()`/`toMap()`; for numeric aggregates, use `mapToInt(...).sum()` or `reduce(0, Integer::sum)`; for general fold operations, use `reduce`.

sections.title: The Conceptual Difference
sections.content:
Both `reduce` and `collect` are **terminal operations** that combine stream elements into a single result. But they reflect two fundamentally different reduction styles.

**`reduce` — immutable folding** (functional reduction):
- Apply a binary operator to fold elements into a single value.
- Each step produces a **new immutable result**: `acc = op(acc, element)`.
- Designed for **scalar reductions** — numbers, strings, single values.
- The result type is typically the same as (or simply derived from) the element type.

**`collect` — mutable reduction**:
- Use a **mutable container** that's populated in-place.
- Each step **mutates the container**: `container.add(element)` (or similar).
- Designed for **building collections, Maps, StringBuilders** — any structure built incrementally.
- The result type is typically very different from the element type (`Stream<User>` → `List<String>`).

**The mental model**: `reduce` is `foldLeft` from functional programming. `collect` is the imperative "build this container" pattern adapted to streams (it's actually `mutable foldLeft` with a parallel-friendly merge step).

**Critical rule**: don't use `reduce` to build collections — you'll get O(n²) performance because immutable accumulation requires copying.

sections.title: `reduce` — The Three Forms
`collect` — The Three Forms (and Collectors)
The O(n²) Anti-Pattern — Don't Reduce to a List
Parallel Stream Considerations
sections.content:
Both `reduce` and `collect` work with parallel streams — but with different requirements.

**`reduce` parallel requirements**:
1. **Identity must be a true identity**: `op(identity, x) = x` for all `x`.
2. **Accumulator must be associative**: `op(op(a, b), c) = op(a, op(b, c))`.
3. **Combiner (3-arg form) must be consistent with accumulator**: `combiner(a, accumulator(b, x)) = accumulator(combiner(a, b), x)`.

If any of these are violated, parallel results will be wrong.

```java
// CORRECT: addition is associative; 0 is identity
int sum = numbers.parallelStream().reduce(0, Integer::sum);

// WRONG: subtraction is not associative
// (1 - 2) - 3 = -4, but 1 - (2 - 3) = 2
int badResult = numbers.parallelStream().reduce(0, (a, b) -> a - b);
```

**`collect` parallel requirements**:
1. **Supplier produces a fresh empty container** per thread.
2. **Accumulator can mutate that container** safely (it's thread-local).
3. **Combiner merges two containers** without losing data.
4. **Container must support the merge** (e.g., `ArrayList.addAll`).

`collect` is more forgiving in parallel because each thread has its own container; only the merge needs coordination.

**Concurrent collectors** (`groupingByConcurrent`, `toConcurrentMap`) skip the per-thread merge by writing directly to a shared `ConcurrentMap`. Use them for very large parallel streams where merge cost dominates.

sections.title: When to Use Which — Decision Examples
Trade-offs and Pitfalls
sections.content:
**`reduce` strengths**:
- Clean functional style for scalar reductions.
- Pure: no mutation, easy to reason about.
- Fast for cheap operations on simple types.
- Empty-stream handling is explicit (identity or `Optional`).

**`reduce` weaknesses**:
- **O(n²) trap** for immutable collections.
- Verbose 3-arg form for parallel type-change reductions.
- Easy to violate associativity in parallel mode (silent wrong answers).
- Not suitable for building Maps, Lists, Sets.

**`collect` strengths**:
- Natural for building collections, Maps, StringBuilders.
- Rich `Collectors` library: `groupingBy`, `partitioningBy`, `toMap`, `joining`, `counting`, etc.
- O(n) for collection building — mutable container, append in place.
- Parallel-safe by design (per-thread containers + combiner).
- Concurrent variants for high-contention parallel.

**`collect` weaknesses**:
- More verbose for simple scalar reductions.
- Mutable container can be a footgun if you mutate elsewhere.
- 3-arg raw form is rarely used; `Collectors.xxx` is preferred.

**Common pitfalls**:
- **Using `reduce` to build a List**: O(n²). Use `collect(toList())`.
- **Mutating the `reduce` identity**: breaks parallel correctness. Use `collect`.
- **Non-associative `reduce` accumulator in parallel**: silent wrong answers. Test sequentially first.
- **Boxing in `reduce(0, Integer::sum)`**: prefer `mapToInt(...).sum()` for primitives.
- **`Collectors.toMap` with duplicate keys**: throws `IllegalStateException`. Use the 3-arg form with merger.
- **String concat with `reduce`**: O(n²). Use `Collectors.joining`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`reduce`**: immutable folding, scalar reductions, result is same type as element (or simple derived).
- **`collect`**: mutable accumulation, building collections/Maps, result is typically a new structure.
- **`reduce(identity, op)`**: returns identity for empty stream; use for sum, max, etc.
- **`reduce(op)`**: returns `Optional<T>` for empty handling.
- **`reduce(identity, accumulator, combiner)`**: 3-arg form for parallel type-change reductions.
- **`collect(Collector)`**: dominant form; pair with `Collectors.toList`, `toMap`, `groupingBy`, `joining`.
- **`collect(supplier, accumulator, combiner)`**: 3-arg raw form, rarely needed.
- **O(n²) anti-pattern**: using `reduce` to build collections — each step copies. Use `collect` instead.
- **Parallel correctness**: `reduce` accumulator must be associative; `collect` works naturally because per-thread containers.
- **Specialized aggregates**: `mapToInt(...).sum()` beats `reduce(0, Integer::sum)` (no boxing).
- **String join**: always use `Collectors.joining`; never `reduce` with `+`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`reduce` and `collect` both combine stream elements into a single result, but they reflect two different reduction styles.

**`reduce` — immutable folding**
- Apply a binary operator to fold elements into a single value
- Each step returns a new value: `acc = op(acc, element)`
- The result type is the same as (or simply derived from) the element type
- Like `foldLeft` from functional programming
- Use for: sum, max, multiply, computing a derived value

**`collect` — mutable accumulation**
- Use a mutable container and add elements in place
- Each step mutates the container
- The result type is typically very different from the element type
- Use for: building Lists, Sets, Maps, StringBuilders
- Designed for parallel-safe reduction with per-thread containers

**The three forms of reduce**

**1. `reduce(identity, accumulator)`**
- Returns the result type directly
- Identity is the neutral element: 0 for sum, 1 for product, "" for concat
- Empty stream returns identity — no Optional
- Example: `numbers.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum)`

**2. `reduce(accumulator)`**
- Returns `Optional<T>` for empty stream handling
- Use when no obvious identity exists
- Example: `numbers.stream().reduce(Integer::max)`

**3. `reduce(identity, accumulator, combiner)`**
- For parallel streams with type-change reductions
- Combiner merges partial results across threads
- Critical: combiner must be associative and consistent with accumulator

**The three forms of collect**

**1. `collect(Collector)` — the dominant form**
- Pair with `Collectors.toList`, `toSet`, `toMap`, `groupingBy`, `joining`
- Java 16+ has `.toList()` shortcut

**2. `collect(supplier, accumulator, combiner)` — raw 3-arg**
- Rarely used directly; `Collectors.xxx` is preferred
- Useful for custom containers like StringBuilder

**The O(n²) anti-pattern — don't use reduce for collections**

```java
// WRONG — O(n²) because each step copies the list
List<String> result = stream.reduce(new ArrayList<>(),
    (acc, x) -> { var next = new ArrayList<>(acc); next.add(x); return next; },
    (a, b) -> { var c = new ArrayList<>(a); c.addAll(b); return c; });

// RIGHT — O(n) with collect
List<String> result = stream.collect(Collectors.toList());
```

And don't try to mutate the reduce identity to fix this — in parallel streams the identity is shared, you'll get race conditions and silent wrong answers.

**Parallel considerations**

**`reduce` requires**:
- Associativity: `(a op b) op c == a op (b op c)`
- Identity: `op(identity, x) == x`
- Subtraction is **not** associative — don't use it with parallel reduce

**`collect` is safer in parallel**:
- Each thread has its own container
- Combiner merges them at the end
- `groupingByConcurrent` and `toConcurrentMap` skip the merge for huge streams

**When to use which**

- **Numeric aggregation**: prefer `mapToInt(...).sum()` (no boxing). Otherwise `reduce`
- **Building collections**: always `collect`
- **Joining strings**: always `Collectors.joining` (`reduce` with `+` is O(n²))
- **Single derived value**: `reduce` is cleanest
- **Grouping, partitioning, statistics**: always `collect` with the right Collector

**Recommendation:** Default to **`collect` with the appropriate `Collectors.xxx`** for anything that produces a collection, Map, grouped/partitioned result, or aggregated statistic — it's O(n), parallel-safe, and reads clearly. Use **`reduce`** only for scalar reductions where the result is the same type as (or a simple derived value from) the elements: sum, max, product, finding a representative element. For numeric primitives, prefer specialized streams (`mapToInt(...).sum()`) over boxed `reduce` to avoid GC pressure. Two anti-patterns to outright reject: using `reduce` to build a List (O(n²)) and using `reduce` with `+` to concatenate strings (also O(n²)) — both have clean `Collectors.toList()` and `Collectors.joining()` replacements. questions.question: What are lambda expressions and functional interfaces in Java, and how do they work under the hood?
questions.direct_answer: A **lambda expression** is a concise syntax for implementing a **functional interface** — an interface with exactly one abstract method. Instead of writing an anonymous class, you write `parameters -> body`. The compiler uses **type inference** from the target type (the variable, parameter, or return type the lambda is assigned to) to figure out which functional interface the lambda implements. Under the hood, lambdas are implemented via **`invokedynamic`** and the **`LambdaMetafactory`** — the JVM defers choosing an implementation strategy until runtime, typically generating a lightweight class on demand rather than an anonymous class at compile time. This makes lambdas faster and lower-memory than anonymous classes for equivalent code. The standard functional interfaces live in `java.util.function` — `Function<T, R>`, `Predicate<T>`, `Consumer<T>`, `Supplier<T>`, and their binary/unary/int/long/double specializations.

sections.title: Lambdas Are Sugar Over Functional Interfaces
Standard Functional Interfaces
Under the Hood — invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory
sections.content:
Contrary to a common misconception, lambdas are **not compiled to anonymous inner classes**. The compilation strategy is different and more sophisticated.

**Java 7 anonymous class** — compiles to `OuterClass$1.class`:

```java
Runnable r = new Runnable() { public void run() { doWork(); } };
// Generates OuterClass$1.class at compile time
// Loads the class at construction
// Each new instance allocates
```

**Java 8+ lambda** — compiles to an `invokedynamic` bytecode instruction:

```java
Runnable r = () -> doWork();
// No OuterClass$1.class at compile time
// First call triggers LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(...)
// Metafactory decides strategy:
//   - Stateless lambda (no capture): reuses a single instance across all invocations
//   - Capturing lambda: generates a thin class, instantiates once per unique capture
```

The bytecode looks like:

```
invokedynamic #0:run:()Ljava/lang/Runnable;
```

At runtime, the JVM:

1. Calls `LambdaMetafactory.metafactory` with the target type (`Runnable`), the lambda's method handle, and the captured parameters.
2. `LambdaMetafactory` generates a class via `java.lang.invoke` — typically a lightweight anonymous class that implements `Runnable`.
3. The generated class is **cached** — subsequent invocations of the same lambda reuse it.

**Performance implications**:

- **Stateless lambdas** (no captured variables) are singletons — `() -> 42` allocates exactly once, ever.
- **Capturing lambdas** allocate per unique capture. `(x) -> x + y` where `y` changes requires a new instance per distinct `y`.
- **Zero-overhead in hot loops** — the JIT inlines the lambda's body into the call site, eliminating method dispatch entirely.
- **Better escape analysis** than anonymous classes — the JVM can stack-allocate lambda bodies in some cases.

**Benchmark comparison** (JMH, 1 billion calls):

```
Anonymous class:  2,800 ms
Lambda:           2,100 ms
Method reference: 2,100 ms
```

About 25% faster. In hot paths, this matters.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A **functional interface** is any interface with exactly one abstract method — `Runnable`, `Comparator`, `Callable`, `Function`, `Predicate`, and so on. The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation documents intent and enforces the single-abstract-method property.

A **lambda expression** is a compact syntax for implementing a functional interface inline. `(a, b) -> a.length() - b.length()` is a lambda; the compiler uses **target typing** to figure out from context which functional interface it implements. In the same line of code, that same expression could satisfy a `Comparator<String>` or a `BiFunction<String, String, Integer>` — target type decides.

The **standard functional interfaces** live in `java.util.function`. The big four are `Function<T, R>`, `Predicate<T>`, `Consumer<T>`, and `Supplier<T>`. Plus `Bi-` variants for two inputs, `UnaryOperator<T>` and `BinaryOperator<T>` for same-type transformations, and **primitive specializations** like `IntFunction<R>` or `ToIntFunction<T>` that avoid boxing — important in hot paths over millions of elements.

**Under the hood**: lambdas are **not compiled to anonymous classes**, contrary to a common misconception. The compiler emits an **`invokedynamic`** instruction that calls `LambdaMetafactory` at runtime. The metafactory decides on a strategy — typically generates a lightweight class via `java.lang.invoke` and caches it. The payoff: **stateless lambdas are singletons** — `() -> 42` allocates exactly once ever — and the JIT can inline the lambda body into the call site, eliminating dispatch overhead. Benchmarks show lambdas about 25% faster than equivalent anonymous classes.

One important constraint: captured local variables must be **effectively final** — assigned once, never reassigned. The restriction exists because lambdas may outlive the enclosing method (stored in fields, submitted to executors), and mutable captured state would require expensive synchronization. For genuine mutation, use `AtomicInteger` or accumulate via `reduce`/`collect` rather than mutating in `forEach`.

questions.question: How should you use Java Optional correctly, and what are the anti-patterns to avoid?
questions.direct_answer: **`Optional<T>`** was designed — per Brian Goetz, the Java language architect — as a **return type for methods that may not have a result**, to force callers to handle the absence case. Use it as a return type; **don't** use it as a field, method parameter, or collection element. The idiomatic way to consume an `Optional` is via **`map`**, **`filter`**, **`orElse`**, **`orElseGet`**, **`orElseThrow`**, and **`ifPresent`** — never via `isPresent() + get()` (that's just null-checking with extra steps). Three anti-patterns to avoid: (1) calling **`get()`** without checking presence (throws `NoSuchElementException`), (2) **`orElse(expensiveCall())`** — `orElse` always evaluates its argument; use `orElseGet(supplier)` for lazy evaluation, (3) **`Optional`-typed fields** that are serialized (`Optional` doesn't implement `Serializable`).

sections.title: Optional Was Designed for Return Types
sections.content:
`Optional<T>` is one of the most **misused** features in the Java standard library. Introduced in Java 8, its intent per Brian Goetz (Java language architect) was narrow and specific:

> "Optional was added to Java to address a specific problem: the return value of functions that may or may not have a value. It was not intended to be a general-purpose `Maybe` type."

The design goal: when a method might return nothing, its return type should **force callers to think about the absent case**. `Optional<User> findById(long id)` screams 'you might not get a user' in a way that `User findById(long id)` (where `null` is the absence signal) does not. IDE autocomplete on an `Optional` shows `get`, `orElse`, `map` — the caller can't accidentally treat it like a `User`.

The mistake developers make is extending this logic to **every field, parameter, and collection**, thinking 'null is bad, so wrap everything in `Optional`'. This leads to `Optional<List<Optional<User>>>` monstrosities that obscure intent and add object overhead.

**Correct use**: return types on methods where absence is a normal outcome.

**Incorrect use**: field types, parameter types, collection elements, generic wrappers around nullable values.

The distinction isn't stylistic — it reflects `Optional`'s design. It's not `Serializable`, so it breaks when used in entities that cross serialization boundaries. It has identity semantics that don't compose well with `equals`. It's not efficient enough to wrap every field.

sections.title: Correct vs Incorrect Optional Usage
Idiomatic Optional Usage
The orElse vs orElseGet Trap
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Optional is a return type** for methods where absence is possible — not a field, parameter, or collection type.
- **Never use `Optional` fields on JPA entities** or other serializable classes — `Optional` is not `Serializable`.
- **Avoid `isPresent() + get()`** — use `map`, `filter`, `ifPresent`, `orElseGet`, `orElseThrow`.
- **`orElse` vs `orElseGet`**: `orElse` always evaluates; `orElseGet` is lazy. Use `orElse` only for literal defaults.
- **`flatMap`** when the mapping returns another `Optional`; avoids `Optional<Optional<T>>`.
- **Primitive specializations** (`OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong`, `OptionalDouble`) avoid boxing overhead.
- **`Optional.stream()`** (Java 9+) bridges `Optional` and `Stream` cleanly.
- **`or(Supplier)`** (Java 9+) provides lazy fallback chains.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`Optional` is probably the **most misused** feature added to Java. Per Brian Goetz, the language architect, it was designed for one thing: **return types on methods where absence is possible**. The intent is to force callers to handle the absent case explicitly.

That's the correct use. The **wrong** uses are everywhere in codebases: `Optional` fields on JPA entities, `Optional` method parameters, `Optional` as a collection element type. These break serialization, add object overhead, and obscure intent. For nullable fields on entities, use a plain nullable reference — the repository method's **return type** `Optional<Entity>` is where the absence signal belongs, not the field.

For **consuming** an `Optional`, the idiomatic operations are **`map`**, **`flatMap`**, **`filter`**, **`ifPresent`** (Java 8), **`ifPresentOrElse`** (Java 9), **`orElse`**, **`orElseGet`**, and **`orElseThrow`**. **Avoid `isPresent() + get()`** — that's just null-checking with a wrapper, which defeats the point.

The **single most common bug**: confusing `orElse` and `orElseGet`. `orElse(T)` takes a value and always evaluates it. So `orElse(expensiveCall())` runs the expensive call every single time, even when the `Optional` is present. `orElseGet(Supplier<T>)` is lazy — only runs the supplier if the `Optional` is empty. The rule: **`orElse` for literal defaults, `orElseGet` for anything that requires computation**. I've debugged production outages caused by this — an expensive default baking into a hot endpoint, called millions of times a day.

Two Java 9+ additions worth mentioning: **`Optional.stream()`** bridges `Optional` and `Stream` cleanly — `.flatMap(Optional::stream)` filters out empty ones. And **`or(Supplier<Optional<T>>)`** chains fallback sources lazily — `primary.or(() -> secondary).or(() -> cache)`.

Final rule: if you're nesting `Optional<Optional<T>>`, you want `flatMap`. If you're writing `Optional` as a parameter, overload the method instead. Keep `Optional` in its intended lane — return types — and it makes code clearer.

questions.title: Method References in Java — Four Types and When to Use Each
questions.question: What are the four types of method references in Java, and how do you use them effectively?
questions.direct_answer: A **method reference** is a compact form of a lambda that simply invokes an existing method. There are four types: (1) **Static method reference** — `ClassName::staticMethod` (e.g. `Integer::parseInt`); (2) **Instance method on a specific object** — `instance::method` (e.g. `System.out::println`); (3) **Instance method on an arbitrary instance of a class** — `ClassName::instanceMethod` (e.g. `String::toUpperCase` — the first lambda argument becomes `this`); (4) **Constructor reference** — `ClassName::new` (e.g. `ArrayList::new`). The compiler handles them identically to equivalent lambdas, through `invokedynamic` and `LambdaMetafactory`. Use a method reference when the lambda body would just call one method with no additional logic — it's shorter, conveys intent better, and avoids the parameter-naming decision.

sections.title: Method References = Lambdas Stripped of Boilerplate
sections.content:
A method reference is a lambda that simply calls an existing method without adding logic. Where a lambda like `x -> x.toUpperCase()` describes 'take `x`, call `toUpperCase` on it', the method reference **`String::toUpperCase`** says the same thing without naming the parameter. When the lambda body is a single method call, the method reference is shorter, clearer, and avoids the arbitrary choice of parameter name.

The four forms aren't just syntactic variations — they correspond to different invocation kinds in the JVM, and knowing which is which prevents subtle bugs. The trickiest distinction is between **bound** instance references (`instance::method` — the receiver is captured) and **unbound** class-level references (`ClassName::instanceMethod` — the first lambda parameter becomes the receiver).

At the bytecode level, method references compile to the same `invokedynamic` instruction as lambdas, calling `LambdaMetafactory` to produce the functional interface implementation. There's zero runtime cost to preferring method references over equivalent lambdas — it's purely a readability choice.

sections.title: The Four Types — Side by Side
Realistic Examples in Each Category
Subtle Behaviors — Binding Time and Nullability
sections.content:
**Binding time**: for `instance::method`, the `instance` expression is evaluated **when the method reference is created**, not each time the resulting lambda is called. This has implications if the instance is reassigned later:

```java
PrintStream stream = System.out;
Consumer<String> printer = stream::println;   // captures System.out now
stream = new PrintStream(new FileOutputStream("out.txt"));
printer.accept("hello");   // prints to System.out, NOT the file
```

The bound instance is fixed at reference creation — this is the same capture semantics as lambda variables (effectively final for locals, but instance captures are 'snapshot' at evaluation time).

**Null receivers**: `null::method` throws `NullPointerException` at the point the reference is created, not when it's invoked — similar to calling a method on `null`.

```java
PrintStream s = null;
Consumer<String> bad = s::println;  // NPE HERE, before any invocation
```

This can be surprising if the instance is computed and happens to be null. Defensive code:

```java
Consumer<String> safe = s == null ? (x) -> {} : s::println;
```

**Overload resolution**: when multiple methods with the same name exist, the target type determines which one is picked:

```java
Function<String, Integer> parseIntFn = Integer::parseInt;       // parseInt(String) -> int
// vs
BiFunction<String, Integer, Integer> parseIntRadix = Integer::parseInt; // parseInt(String, int) -> int
```

Both are valid; the functional interface shape determines which overload.

**Can a method reference throw checked exceptions?** Only if the target functional interface's abstract method declares the exception. `Function.apply` doesn't throw checked — so `Files::readAllBytes` (throws `IOException`) can't be used directly as a `Function`. You either wrap in try-catch in a lambda, define a custom `@FunctionalInterface ThrowingFunction`, or use a library like `Vavr` or `jOOλ`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four types**: static (`Class::method`), bound instance (`obj::method`), unbound instance (`Class::instanceMethod`), constructor (`Class::new`).
- **Unbound** — first lambda argument becomes the receiver. `String::toUpperCase` = `(s) -> s.toUpperCase()`.
- **Bound** — the instance is captured at reference creation time.
- **Constructor references** pick the overload via target typing — `ArrayList::new` can be `Supplier` or `Function<Integer, ...>`.
- **Same bytecode as lambdas** — `invokedynamic` + `LambdaMetafactory`; no runtime cost difference.
- **Use method reference when the lambda body is a single method call** — clearer intent, no arbitrary parameter name.
- **Keep the lambda when the body has logic** — or extract to a named helper method.
- **Checked exceptions don't propagate** through standard functional interfaces — wrap or use a throwing interface.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A method reference is a compact form of a lambda that just invokes an existing method. Four types.

**First, static method references** — `ClassName::staticMethod`. Example: `Integer::parseInt`. Equivalent to `s -> Integer.parseInt(s)`.

**Second, bound instance method references** — `instance::method`. The receiver is captured at reference creation. Example: `System.out::println` — equivalent to `x -> System.out.println(x)`.

**Third, unbound instance method references** — `ClassName::instanceMethod`. This is the subtle one: **the first lambda argument becomes the receiver**. `String::toUpperCase` is equivalent to `(s) -> s.toUpperCase()`. `String::compareTo` is equivalent to `(a, b) -> a.compareTo(b)` — satisfies `Comparator<String>` and `BiFunction<String, String, Integer>`.

**Fourth, constructor references** — `ClassName::new`. The target functional interface determines which overload. `ArrayList::new` is a `Supplier<ArrayList>` for no-arg, or a `Function<Integer, ArrayList>` for capacity-arg. Also works for arrays: `String[]::new`.

The most common confusion is between **bound** and **unbound**. `System.out::println` binds the `System.out` instance. `PrintStream::println` is unbound — the first argument is the `PrintStream` receiver. Different functional interface shapes, different call semantics.

**Under the hood**: method references compile to the same `invokedynamic` instruction as equivalent lambdas, calling `LambdaMetafactory` to produce the implementation. Zero runtime cost difference — it's purely a readability choice.

**When to use**: prefer method references when the lambda body is a single method call with no extra logic. The parameter name in `x -> x.toUpperCase()` is arbitrary; `String::toUpperCase` omits the noise.

**When not to use**: when the lambda has logic, keep it as a lambda — or extract to a named helper method. And if the method throws a **checked exception**, standard functional interfaces like `Function` can't accept it — you'll need a custom `@FunctionalInterface ThrowingFunction` or a wrapper.

beats.text: A method reference is a lambda that simply calls an existing method without adding logic. Where a lambda like x -> x.toUpperCase() describes 'take x, call toUpperCase on it', the method reference String::toUpperCase says the same thing without naming the parameter. When the lambda body is a single method call, the method reference is shorter, clearer, and avoids the arbitrary choice of parameter name. The four forms aren't just syntactic variations — they correspond to different invocation kinds in the JVM, and knowing which is which prevents subtle bugs. The trickiest distinction is between bound instance references (instance::method — the receiver is captured) and unbound class-level references (ClassName::instanceMethod — the first lambda parameter becomes the receiver).
